set.approach: The cirque is a basin on the east face of Pikes Peak, reached from the summit-road end by dropping onto Barr Trail and following it down to the A-frame shelter. From there contour at roughly the same height across to the north side of the basin and drop in. The couloir is the final major line in a steep-walled ravine along the cirque's northern edge, and a rock step at a choke point partway up is the landmark that identifies it. The slopes are steep and exposed to avalanches in winter and spring, so check the avalanche forecast.

review.notes: Approach from the area page (Barr Trail, A-frame, contour, drop in from north side); landmark from the route page. Distances and elevations left out (single source). Descent not stated, so none written.

set.approach: Park at the sharp bend roughly a mile below the summit on Pikes Peak Highway, the first switchback beyond the pullout serving the two popular ice routes nearby. Walk over the road and follow the cog railway bed downhill for a short way to an obvious saddle on the left. Leave the tracks, cross the saddle hugging its left side, and slip into a steep chute that has a big cave high on it. Descend most of its length, then angle left over the spur and contour round to a spot beneath the yellow wall mid-spur; the route is in the big wall above.

review.notes: Single route page for the approach. Distances left out. The page does not say how parties get off after the upper pitches, so no descent written.

set.approach: From The Crags trailhead, follow the Crags Trail and take the right fork onto the Devil's Playground Trail, then continue up to Devil's Playground and keep on toward the summit to the Rock Wall pullout. Descend steep to moderate snow down the French Creek drainage, keeping the Moontower and Sphinx Buttress on your left, until you reach the foot of the buttress. It lies on the southern flank of the cirque; get on it through a weakness right of its base. A different line of approach skirts the north ridge of the cirque from Devil's Playground and comes in from the Elk Park trailhead. The descent into the cirque is leeward and wind-loaded, so check the avalanche forecast.
set.descent_text: From the last belay ledge, exit up and left, then downclimb on the side below the Moontower and return to the road. Finishing over the Moontower itself is an option for parties who want the summit.

review.notes: Approach from the Sphinx Buttress and French Creek area pages; descent from the route page. Mileage and gain omitted (single source). Descent wording is vague in the source, kept general.

set.approach: The couloir lies in the Summit Lake cirque below the summit of Mt. Blue Sky, just left of the large Sunrise Couloir. From the Summit Lake parking area, circle the lake on its south side and climb the slope into the bowl; the approach is short. It is the couloir that looks steep and narrow when you face Sunrise. The line sees sun, so snow can soften and the cirque is exposed to avalanches; check the avalanche forecast.
set.descent_text: Parties can glissade the Sunrise Couloir, keeping clear of the cornice that builds over its top, or walk down either Spalding Ridge or Evans Ridge. Spalding is typically the quicker of the two.

review.notes: Route page for location relative to Sunrise and the descent options; area page for the walk into the bowl. Road season and reservations left out as current conditions.

set.approach: Reach the Indian Trail #500 trailhead off the Copper King road, high on the plateau edge, and hike down the trail for a distance. Leave it and bushwhack southwest down a steep, scrub-oak gully of dirt and scree to the floor of North Fork Tabeguache Creek; several gullies are possible but not all go through. Once on the creek floor, turn right and go a short distance upstream to reach the falls. Winter access to the trailhead is difficult, so confirm the route in with the land manager.
set.descent_text: Climb to the small tree where the creek levels off above the falls and rappel from it; a single long rope is needed, and a shorter one will not reach the bottom. Alternatively wander further up the streambed, which holds a short ice step.

review.notes: Route page for the trail/bushwhack and tree anchor. Mileages, gully angle and rope length omitted (single source). Road-status details omitted as current conditions.

set.approach: Start at the Glacier Gorge trailhead in Rocky Mountain National Park. In winter use the shortcut that branches off shortly past the second bridge, ahead of the fork where Loch Vale and Mills Lake diverge, and bear left toward Mills Lake. From the lake wander up and to the left to the bowl at the base of the wide flow on the northeast side of Thatchtop; the flow sits directly above the bowl. Deep snow after a storm can make the lake approach slow, and the slopes carry avalanche exposure, so check the avalanche forecast.
set.descent_text: From the top of the ice, traverse left along Thatchtop's shoulder, cross a ridge, and go down Class 2 talus on its other side. Work down until the bowl lies just below, go through a notch in the ridge, and take a couloir to the basin at the foot of the climb. Parties who bail after the third pitch can escape left along a wide ledge of talus or snow and join the same descent.

review.notes: Approach from the area page, base location from the route page; descent from the route page. Distances left out.

set.approach: Start at the Glacier Gorge trailhead in Rocky Mountain National Park. In winter take the shortcut that leaves the trail just after the second bridge, before the Loch Vale and Mills Lake split, and head left toward Mills Lake, then wander up and to the left. The route is a steep pillar-like curtain a couple of hundred yards right of All Mixed Up when seen from below. You can walk around to its base or climb two very easy pitches of ice to reach it. The slopes carry avalanche exposure, so check the avalanche forecast.
set.descent_text: Rappel from a tree to the climber's left of the ice. A short stretch of steep brush leads from the top of the ice to the trees.

review.notes: Route page for position and the tree rappel; area page for the shortcut and lake approach. The route's grade is described inconsistently on the page; text is grade-neutral.

set.approach: Start at the Glacier Gorge trailhead in Rocky Mountain National Park. In winter take the shortcut that leaves the trail just after the second bridge, before the Loch Vale and Mills Lake split, and head left to Mills Lake. The route is the middle, lower-angle bit of blue ice on the slope just above the lake, far below All Mixed Up. A belay stance with rock anchors sits to its left.
set.descent_text: Walk off by way of a fairly steep gully on the right, skirting the neighbouring ice.

review.notes: Single route page for location and the walk-off; area page for the trail. No distances.

set.approach: Start at the Glacier Gorge trailhead in Rocky Mountain National Park. In winter take the shortcut that leaves the trail just after the second bridge, before the Loch Vale and Mills Lake split, and head left toward Mills Lake, then wander up and to the left to the upper cliff. The route is to the left of Dazed and Confused, along the left side of the leftmost curtain, starting in a corner. The slopes carry avalanche exposure, so check the avalanche forecast.

review.notes: Route page for position; area page for the trail. Descent not stated, none written.

set.approach: Start at the Glacier Gorge trailhead in Rocky Mountain National Park. In winter take the shortcut that leaves the trail just after the second bridge, before the Loch Vale and Mills Lake split, and head left to Mills Lake. The route is the right-hand bit of ice on the slope just above the lake, far below All Mixed Up. In a busy winter the lake is reached without flotation, though the last stretch up to the ice can be snow-wallowing.
set.descent_text: Go down the fairly steep gully off to the right. The belay tree is up and left of the ice, with a stump above the ice that can be slung on the way.

review.notes: Single route page for location and descent; area page for the trail.

set.approach: Approach from the South Colony Lakes side of the Sangre de Cristo Range: a long jeep road leads to the original trailhead, then the trail continues up to the lakes. The route is the left of two couloir systems on the northeast wall of Crestone Needle, well left of the Ellingwood Arete and just left of where the Full Ledges variation starts, less than a half mile west of the lower lake. The couloir is steep and holds avalanche-prone snow, so check the avalanche forecast.

review.notes: Route page for the location of the couloir, area page for the access. Distances and road details omitted. The page says the couloir ends near the regular route, but does not describe the descent, so none written.

set.approach: Take the Coal Basin Road beyond Redstone to where it ends at the winter closure. A trail switchbacks steeply up the slope on the south side of the road, starting a short way down from the closure and nearly across from the parking. Follow it to the cave. The route is the obvious bolted line at the top of the approach trail, with easier ice to its left and a harder overhanging mixed line to its right. Hanging ice at the cave can fall, so watch for it.

review.notes: Area page for the road and trail, route page for the line. Descent not stated for this bolted line, none written.

set.approach: Park at the Mt. Lindsey trailhead on the Upper Huerfano road. A short way back down the road from it, find a way down the slope across the gully, then hike northeast up to the broad central ice flow on the west-facing slope. The route is on the upper tier in the centre. Reach it by climbing any of the lower-tier lines, then belay from trees below the upper tier. A snowfield above the climb can send avalanches, so check the avalanche forecast.

review.notes: Area pages for the trailhead and gully approach, route page for the tier and avalanche note. Descent not stated, none written.

set.approach: Park at the Mt. Lindsey trailhead on the Upper Huerfano road. A short way back down the road from it, find a way down the slope across the gully, then hike northeast up to the broad central ice flow on the west-facing slope. The route is on the left side of the lower tier, where several lines are possible. A snowfield above the upper tier can send avalanches, so check the avalanche forecast.
set.descent_text: A walk-off exists leftward between the tiers. The belay for the lower tier is a tree near the upper tier.

review.notes: Route page for the walk-off between tiers; area pages for the approach.

set.approach: Park at the Mt. Lindsey trailhead on the Upper Huerfano road. A short way back down the road from it, find a way down the slope across the gully, then hike northeast up to the broad central ice flow on the west-facing slope. This route is on the far right side of the ice. A snowfield above the upper tier can send avalanches, so check the avalanche forecast.

review.notes: Area pages for the approach, route page for its position. Descent not stated, none written.

set.approach: Start from the Bighorn Creek trailhead and hike up the drainage to the Dollie Mine Cabin, a common place to sleep before the climb. The waterfall is visible from the cabin and lies a short way uphill and east of it. A mineshaft sits just below the route and makes a handy place to gear up. The right side of the flow is easier and the left side harder. Check the avalanche forecast before entering the drainage in winter.

review.notes: Single route page. Mileage and distance from the cabin omitted. Descent not stated, none written.

set.approach: Start from the parking at the switchback on the North Henson Road west of Lake City, then hike steeply up to the gate and follow the fence line to the back corner of the private land. Continue west along the old road bed or trail, cross the pass, and drop to upper Cow Creek. Follow the path of least resistance down the creek, generally on its east side, then make an ascending traverse west-northwest into the drainage that comes in from the unnamed lake below Dragon's Back, up to the cliff band. The terrain is serious avalanche country, so check the avalanche forecast.
set.descent_text: Rappel the route, which is recommended, or hike north above the cliffs to reach neighbouring climbs, or walk off to the south. A long rope is needed for the rappel, and a V-thread tool may be handy. Save energy for the hike back out over the pass.

review.notes: Route page for the approach and descent options, area page for the trailhead and gate. Distances, elevations and rope length left out (single source).

set.approach: Start from the parking at the switchback on the North Henson Road west of Lake City, hike up to the gate, follow the fence line round the private land, then continue west on the old road bed over the pass and down to upper Cow Creek. Follow the easiest ground down to the foot of the drainage beneath Blackwall Mountain's eastern bowl, the next drainage over to the north from Dragon's Tail, and walk up into the amphitheater. The route is the rightmost of three flows above a broad low-angle slab. It sits in an avalanche funnel, so check the avalanche forecast.
set.descent_text: Make a long rappel from the tree at the top, if it is still there, then either downclimb or rope down the remaining gentle slab. Carry two ropes and a V-thread tool.

review.notes: Route page for position and descent, area page for the trailhead and gate. Distances, elevations left out.

set.approach: From the Wetterhorn Basin trailhead, stroll briefly south on the trail until the first ditch crossing, where a drainage enters from the east. Go east-southeast alongside the ditch and into the trees, threading through the fallen timber. Higher up in the trees the drainage splits without much warning, and the left fork goes nowhere useful, so keep an eye on the low ridge to the south. The flow lies a short distance east of the trail, a casual approach by local standards.
set.descent_text: A small tree set back from the lip serves as the anchor. Rappel from it, or walk off to the left.

review.notes: Single route page for both; area page for the trailhead. Distances and rope length omitted.

set.approach: The ice forms where the gulch drops over a cliff just above the river. The top approach starts at the point where the highway crosses Cataract Gulch, south of town: park off the pavement nearby, then follow the creek down, bypassing steeper sections on the right and staying near the watercourse. You can rope down the climb from trees, or keep walking down and to the right to arrive at its base. The creek approach is exposed to localised avalanches and should be avoided when hazard is high; check the avalanche forecast. From below, the river usually cannot be crossed safely.
set.descent_text: Either climb back out to the highway, or walk off leftward (as you face the ice) down to the river.

review.notes: Single route page for access and descent. Distances and elevation drop omitted.

set.approach: Park on the left near the reservoir just past the Mayflower Gulch trailhead on the road toward Leadville. Hike to the foot of the first large couloir cutting the east side of the Wheeler ridge. It begins as a tight couloir between two rock walls and then opens to a large snowfield. The couloir is steep snow terrain with avalanche exposure, so check the avalanche forecast.

review.notes: Parking from area page, position of the couloir from the route page. Distance omitted (single source). The route page does not say how parties descend, so none written.

set.approach: Park on the left near the reservoir just past the Mayflower Gulch trailhead on the road toward Leadville. From there go south across the lake, passing the first large couloir cutting the east side, and continue to a V-shaped couloir that usually holds ice. Climb through its choke and a bit of snow above; the route starts on the face to the south. The couloir is avalanche terrain, so check the avalanche forecast.
set.descent_text: Descend the face the way you came, or traverse south across the snowfield and go down a very steep couloir.

review.notes: Route page for the approach and descent options, area page for parking.

set.approach: Start at Engineer Pass and head north across American Flats, then descend Wildhorse Creek toward the drop where the creek falls into a compact amphitheater. To get to the ice from below, skirt the cliff on the west side of the creek. The alternative is to build an anchor above and rappel in. The amphitheater holds a handful of flows, and the best is probably the wall on the climber's left. The approach is long and remote, and the slopes above carry avalanche risk, so check the avalanche forecast.

review.notes: Route page for approach, area page for the Engineer Pass starting point. Distance omitted (single source). Descent not stated apart from the rappel-in alternative, none written.

set.approach: Start at Engineer Pass and head north across American Flats, then descend northwest into Wildhorse Creek. Pass Crazy Horse on the west side and keep following the creek down, then angle east-northeast above a deep cut to the side drainage coming off Blackwall Mountain. Walk to the lip of the ice and rappel in, or go down the inset gully to the bottom and carry your gear back up. The setting is remote and avalanche terrain lies above it, so check the avalanche forecast.
set.descent_text: The ice tops out at trees with ample anchors. After the climb, the way out is a long hike back up to American Flats.

review.notes: Single route page for route-specific detail, area page for the starting point. Elevations and mileage omitted.

set.approach: From the Williams Creek trailhead, contour northeast to meet Williams Creek, or follow the streambed itself if it is frozen or snowed over. Continue up the creek until the canyon tightens and turns sharply east, then look to the right (south) for a side canyon that seems to end in an abrupt headwall. Go up into it to the first ice, which is hidden on the left wall. In winter the trailhead is a long way in from where the plowed road ends. Check the avalanche forecast.
set.descent_text: After the final column, rappel from live trees above and left of it. Parties can instead climb out of the canyon to the south, reaching the saddle just east of the conspicuous knoll, then follow the drainage south-southwest to the main creek.

review.notes: Single route page for approach and descent options, area page for trailhead. Distances, heights and rope length omitted.

set.approach: Use the Rock of Ages trailhead off Colorado 145 west of Telluride, reached by Silver Pick Road and then a forest road to its end. Hike south on the trail, forking right onto the Elk Creek trail where the Rock of Ages trail splits off. Above treeline the trail passes under the north ridge of Fowler Peak, formerly Big Bear Peak. After a couple of talus crossings, leave the trail and work up along the bottom margin of the rock glacier into the basin under the northwest face. The couloir is deeply inset, in plain view once you are in the cirque. It holds avalanche-prone snow, so check the avalanche forecast.
set.descent_text: Three ways down are used. One heads east on Class 2 to 3 ground toward the neighbouring point, descends its northwest face on moderate snow below the west shoulder, and follows the old mining road to the Elk Creek trail. Another carries on farther east down to the saddle that the Rock of Ages trail crosses. The third is a loose, tedious Class 3 to 4 traverse west to Boskoff Peak, then down the wide gully on the peak's north side, just east of the top, to meet the Elk Creek trail. Rockfall is a hazard, so start early.

review.notes: Single route page for both trailhead and descent options; area page confirms the Telluride/CO 145 access. Elevations and mileage omitted.
